keycloak/keycloakx.summary: Keycloak (Quarkus). It brings no database of its own: by default it uses a development database inside the pod, which is not for real use.
guide: Database: for anything beyond a trial, give Keycloak a PostgreSQL. Pick "My own PostgreSQL" and enter where it is; the password is read from a Secret that already exists in the install namespace, so it never passes through this form.

Access: the chart can publish Keycloak through an Ingress. Keycloak serves under /auth by default; behind an Ingress with TLS the chart's proxy setting (already on) makes it trust the forwarded headers.
Create the admin account after the first start (the chart prints how in its notes).

keycloak/keycloak.summary: Keycloak (legacy, WildFly-based chart). It installs its own PostgreSQL unless you point it at yours.
guide: This chart is the older WildFly-based Keycloak. If you can, prefer "keycloakx", which is maintained for current Keycloak versions.

Database: by default the chart starts its own PostgreSQL next to Keycloak. To use one you already run, pick "My own PostgreSQL": the bundled one is switched off and Keycloak is given your database through environment variables; the password is read from an existing Secret.

set.value:
- name: DB_VENDOR
  value: postgres
- name: DB_ADDR
  value: "{host}"
- name: DB_PORT
  value: "{port}"
- name: DB_DATABASE
  value: "{database}"
- name: DB_USER
  value: "{username}"
- name: DB_PASSWORD
  valueFrom:
    secretKeyRef:
      name: "{passwordSecret}"
      key: "{passwordKey}"

gitea/gitea.summary: Gitea (self-hosted Git). The chart starts a highly available PostgreSQL by default, which is heavy for a small install.
guide: Database: the default is a PostgreSQL cluster of several pods. For a small install pick "Bundled single PostgreSQL"; to use a database you already run, pick "My own PostgreSQL" — the password comes from an existing Secret.
Access: Git over SSH needs its own port (the chart's ssh service); the Ingress below only carries the web interface.

minio-aistor/aistor-operator.summary: MinIO AIStor's operator: the controller that runs AIStor object stores. It needs a licence from MinIO (SUBNET); install it first, then install an object store (the aistor-objectstore chart).
guide: Licence: the operator reads it from a Secret named minio-license (key minio.license) in its own namespace. Paste the licence here and the Secret is created for you — or point at one that already exists. Use the decoded licence (it starts with eyJ), not the encrypted block (it starts with ZXlK).
Without a licence the operator starts, but the object stores it runs refuse S3 requests until one is installed.
after: The operator runs in {namespace}. Now install an object store: Marketplace → minio-aistor → aistor-objectstore.

options.note: The name is fixed: it is where the operator looks.

fields.label: Licence Secret
fields.help: Paste the licence below to create it, copy one from another namespace, or leave an existing Secret as it is.

paste.hint: A MinIO licence is a JWT that starts with eyJ. A block that starts with ZXlK is the encrypted one — use the decoded licence.

options.title: I'll add the licence later
options.note: The operator starts; the object stores it runs refuse S3 requests until a Secret named minio-license exists in this namespace.

minio-aistor/aistor-objectstore.summary: A MinIO AIStor object store, run by the AIStor operator (install the aistor-operator chart first, with a licence).
guide: Size: the chart's default is 4 servers with 4 drives each — sixteen volumes, which is a real cluster. For a home or test cluster pick the single-server option.
Root credentials: the object store reads them from a Secret. Create one here with a generated password (nothing is typed into the Helm values).
after: The object store {release} in {namespace} comes up when its pods are ready. Its S3 API is the Service {release}-hl / minio on port 9000, the console on 9001 — see the Routing page to publish it.
The root user and its password are in the Secret you chose (key config.env); read them on the Secrets page (reading a value is audited).

fields.help: Created with the button below (user minioadmin, a generated password, key config.env); or name one that exists.

options.title: A Secret I made myself
options.note: It must hold the key config.env: export MINIO_ROOT_USER="…" and export MINIO_ROOT_PASSWORD="…", one per line.

options.title: One server, one drive (home / test)
options.note: No redundancy: if the volume is lost the data is.

options.title: The chart's default: 4 servers × 4 drives
options.note: Sixteen volumes of 10 GiB. Needs at least four nodes' worth of room to be useful.

ot-container-kit/redis.summary: A Redis instance run by the Redis operator (install the redis-operator chart first). By default it has no password at all.
guide: Operator: this chart only describes the instance; the redis-operator chart (same repository) must already be running in the cluster, or nothing starts.

Access: pick a password, or an ACL setup — the default user keeps a generated password for the operator and a named user gets its own for your applications. Both are generated into the Secret; nothing is typed into the Helm values.
after: The Redis {release} in {namespace} comes up when its pods are ready (the operator creates them). Reach it on the Service {release} port 6379.
The passwords are in the Secret you chose; read them on the Secrets page (reading a value is audited). With ACL, applications sign in as the named user with its password key (<user>-password).

fields.label: Secret for the password

options.title: ACL: a named user for applications
options.note: The operator keeps signing in as the default user with its own password; applications use the named user (user app, all commands) — narrow it later with ACL SETUSER.

options.title: No password
options.note: Anyone who can reach the Service can use it. Only inside a trusted cluster.
